Have you ever butted heads with a partner because you wanted to plan a jam-packed vacation itinerary and they preferred to lounge on the beach? Have you ever argued with family or friends about whether to book a local Airbnb or an all-inclusive resort? When flying solo, you don't need to worry about these dilemmas — and that's far from the only benefit of solo travel.

However, planning a trip on your own can feel daunting, especially if it's your first time. That's why I've rounded up some of TPG's favorite destinations for first-time solo travelers. No matter what kind of traveler you are and what you're looking for on your maiden voyage, this list is sure to inspire you.

Related: The 12 best places to travel solo

While Mexico often conjures images of all-inclusive hotels and long beach days, the cultural and culinary hub of Oaxaca goes deeper. TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews just got back from a solo trip here and raves about the travel-worthy food scene and captivating art and history.

“The historic center of Oaxaca is easily walkable and full of coffee shops, art galleries and ceramic stores to pop in and out of at your own pace and convenience,” she says. “It was also super easy to make friends on the few tours I booked — I did a nighttime street food tour with Culinary Backstreets and a long day trip to Hierve del Agua that I booked on Viator, and I ended up running into the people I met at bakeries and markets the rest of the week.”

Related: 5 detour destinations in Mexico beyond the tourist hot spots

Whatever type of solo trip you’re dreaming of, France is worth considering.

TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson recommends Paris. It may be known as the City of Love, but that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy it on your own — especially if you’re a foodie or art lover. Snack on fresh-baked croissants in between museum visits (the Musee du quai Branly, which features non-Western art from around the world, is a must-see).

If you’d prefer a slower pace, Lauren Wassum raves about Provence: “There are plenty of villages to explore where you can get in touch with yourself through slow and intentional living.” But this isn’t to say there is nothing to do. “You can walk Van Gogh’s footsteps in Arles and Saint-Rémy, take a provencal cooking class or even tour the lavender fields when in they are in bloom in the Luberon Valley.”

To really push yourself out of your comfort zone, try Japan for your first solo trip. Japan’s culture and traditions are so different from the U.S., it will catapult you out of your day-to-day life a little faster than most destinations.

TPG senior writer Tanner Saunders loves the Land of the Rising Sun as a solo destination. “Tokyo is massive, sure, but it's relatively easy to figure out how to get around, the people are mostly so kind, it's super safe and dining alone is so common.” And don’t worry if you can’t read Japanese; English is common in most tourist areas.

Japan may seem small, but its islands are incredibly diverse. There’s something for every type of traveler — from the snow-dusted ski capital of Hokkaido to the southernmost island of Okinawa, sometimes known as “the Hawaii of Japan.”

Related: When is the best time to visit Japan?

Senior editor Christine Gallipeau recommends New Zealand for first-time solo travelers, citing the country’s safety record and the Kiwis’ trademark friendliness.

“I was there during the Rugby World Cup and had a last-minute issue with lodging,” she says. “One of the local airports let me and my friends just crash in the rental car office for the night, and later in Wellington, a stranger opened their home to us since hostels and hotels were sold out.”

It takes a while to get here, but you’ll be rewarded with peace, quiet and the sense of being truly alone.

Most visitors agree road tripping is the best way to see New Zealand, so you’ll need to rent a car (and be prepared to drive on the left side). You can see the highlights in just a few days, or spend weeks exploring and not run out of things to do.

Related: Explore some of New Zealand's most beautiful regions at these Rosewood lodges

If you’d like to stay a little closer to home for your first solo trip, Costa Rica is relatively easy to reach from the U.S. while still feeling a world away.

It’s among Latin America’s most popular solo travel destinations thanks, in part, to its friendly locals. “Everyone is sooo welcoming,” says TPG social media manager Maren Gimnes, “plus it’s safe and easy to get around.”

With beaches on one side and wildlife-rich rainforests on the other, not to mention volcanoes and hot springs, solo travelers can get their fill of both relaxation and adventure.

Try basing yourself in Tamarindo if you’re after sun, surf and sand. If wildlife is your main goal, head to Monteverde Cloud Forest or Manuel Antonio National Park. Thrill seekers will want to focus on La Fortuna, the country’s adventure capital.

Related: How to visit Costa Rica on points and miles

Many European cities are great candidates for first-time solo trips, but Ireland’s lively capital city stands out for its welcoming pub culture and manageable size. TPG social media manager Annie Black loves it because Dublin is “very easy to navigate and has lots of fun free things to do.”

If you’re hoping to socialize with locals and fellow travelers, Dublin’s welcoming pub culture is a must. Head to the bustling Temple Bar neighborhood (or any pub, really) for a pint of Guinness or Bulmer’s and some foot-stomping trad music.

Plus, plentiful day trips and group tours make it easy for solo travelers to explore nearby attractions like the gorgeous Wicklow Mountains and the jaw-dropping Giant’s Causeway without the hassle of renting a car.

Related: What it's like flying Aer Lingus business class across the Atlantic

If you’re ready to venture a little farther afield, TPG principal Eric Rosen highlights Cape Town as a great spot for first-time visitors, saying it’s “very navigable and safe for solo travelers.”

Cape Town has all the benefits of a city trip plus easy access to outdoor pursuits like hiking, mountain bike trails, beaches and even penguins. Rideshares are readily available and affordable for getting around town, or you can easily explore outside the city by renting a car, hiring a driver or joining an organized group tour.

Sea Point and De Waterkant/Green Point neighborhoods are great choices for solo travelers wanting a safe, walkable base close to the beach. If you’d rather be within easy reach of the restaurant and bar scene on Kloof Street, try Tamboerskloof.

Related: Africa's first Edition hotel is opening in Cape Town next year

Vietnam is a Southeast Asian sliver of adventure, culture and more. Plus, it’s quite affordable — even if you’re not splitting the cost of your hotel with a travel companion. Most meals will run you between $5 and $10.

There’s truly something for everyone: The UNESCO World Heritage Site of Ha Long Bay; the delightfully chaotic capital of Hanoi; and the hip beach town of Da Nang, where expats from all over the world relax.

You won’t want to leave without sampling some of the local cuisine. There’s pho and banh mi, of course, but don’t miss other local dishes like bun cha (pork with dipping broth) and cha ca (turmeric-marinated fish). Wash it all down with a beer at Hanoi’s Train Street, where you can eat while watching an active railway run back and forth inches from your trackside café.

Related: A new Hilton just opened one of Vietnam's best cities

There’s a reason (several, in fact) that Iceland is a perennial favorite for solo travelers. English is nearly ubiquitous, and the country’s manageable size and well-developed infrastructure make it easy to get around. It’s also one of the safest countries on the planet — so safe, it’s said Iceland has more horses than police officers.

Nature lovers can bask in a huge variety of landscapes, from hiking across glaciers to soaking in geothermal hot springs to snorkeling between tectonic plates. Meanwhile, travelers seeking nightlife and connection can revel in downtown Reykjavik, which also has a booming LGBTQIA+ scene.

“You really can’t go wrong with any Nordic country,” TPG managing editor Lyndsey Matthews says. “English is widely spoken, plus they’re all very safe countries, so I’ve always been comfortable whether it’s a super remote destination or a big city.”

Related: Delta Air Lines adds Iceland nonstops from Boston hub

Whether you’re looking for epic underwater adventures or a few days of beach bumming, look no further than the Central American oasis of Belize.

Despite its small size, Belize has a big reputation for some of the world’s best snorkeling and scuba diving. Check some adventures off your bucket list by diving the Great Blue Hole or swimming with nurse sharks in Shark Ray Alley.

If you’d rather spend your vacation on land — perhaps in a hammock with a good book and a cold drink — head out on a ferry to one of the many islands, or cays, like car-free Caye Caulker. The island's motto is “Go Slow,” and that’s all you need to know.

Related: Belize's best all-inclusive resorts

When traveling solo, you can go, do, see and eat exactly what you choose — whether that's a culture-filled city trip, an epic outdoor adventure, a relaxing beach break or a little of everything. This list has all the above so you can choose your dream solo destination.

Need more inspo for your first solo trip? Don't miss our roundups of the best places to travel solo in the US, the top destinations for a solo weekend getaway and the best cruise lines for solo travelers.

#5947. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#5946. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#5945. Joe Biden Flew Cape Air For Thanksgiving—His Airport Cart Ride Turned Into A Political Fight

Joe Biden carried his bag through Philadelphia airport, got onto a police cart, and wound up at the center of another argument about the 2024 election. Biden and his wife Jill were headed to Nantucket for Thanksgiving. The final leg of the trip was on Cape Air. The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive. Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage: View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property. View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book: Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down. The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.” But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.” I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him. He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family. In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort. We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency. Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017 George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office. There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman. A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there. The former president turned 84 on Friday. He’s dealing with cancer. And he’s still traveling commercially with his wife, albeit with a security detail and a little more help getting through the terminal than most passengers receive.

Shakiah Davis posted this video with the caption, “Ran into Joe and his wife today at the PHL…..” Biden walks slowly, carrying a tan leather duffel, then takes a seat on a Philadelphia Police electric cart. Jill is seated on another cart. Here’s the version without the political argument pasted over the footage:

View Shakiah Davis’s video of Joe and Jill Biden at Philadelphia airport

The Carry On store visible behind Biden is at the top of Philadelphia’s B concourse, next to Passyunk Steaks. This is familiar territory for American Airlines passengers. The Bidens arrived on Nantucket Sunday evening, November 22, on Cape Air from Boston. That was their arrival airline last Thanksgiving, too. Their family tradition of spending the holiday on the island dates to 1975, and they’re staying again at David Rubenstein’s waterfront property.

View Nantucket Current’s video of the Bidens’ Thanksgiving arrival

Earlier this month he explained why he was cutting back appearances for his new book:

Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.

The version of the airport video reposted by Western Journal uses it to revisit claims that Biden could have handled another four years in office. The comments on the cleaner version include “Yeah, he could’ve served another 4 years” and Nick Shirley’s “Put him back in office he’s ready for another 4.”

But “The guy is fighting cancer………” had more than 23,000 likes when I checked, substantially more than either of those comments. Even under the political repost, one response was, “Not a fan but will pray for him and his family.”

I’ve long viewed Biden as an honorable man and a poor president. He let his administration operate like a feudal system, with interest groups controlling their policy areas. That made for bad policy and bad politics, pulling him away from the median voters who elected him.

He also wasn’t up to another term. Pretending otherwise delayed a real process to choose his successor, and handing the nomination to Kamala Harris left his party poorly positioned for the election. She was a terrible candidate. But the debate made the problem clear, and he dropped out. A video of him taking an airport cart more than two years doesn’t tell us anything new. Now he’s an airline passenger going to see his family.

In June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort.

We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency.

Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017

George W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office.

There are still airline issues worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman.

A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there.

#5944. A Glorious Man

Even now, Ben Sasse has not stopped thinking and speaking and writing about America.

Former senator Ben Sasse speaks during an event in Washington, D.C., June 2, 2026.

Listen closely, and you will notice that Ben Sasse uses the word “glorious” often. He uses it for the everyday goodness of Americans, the architecture of limited government they inherited, and now for his own rendezvous with God. Death by metastatic pancreatic cancer, Sasse says, is “what I need.”

This historian by training, turnaround specialist by trade, former senator by a felt obligation, is the rare conservative undeterred by fatalism, even — especially — when staring it in the face. In wisdom tucked into a footnote in his second book, Sasse doesn’t deny that the world is a “broken place always at risk of spinning out of control.” It’s just that he finds this unruliness quieting in a way, and responds with “profound gratitude for the gifts we’ve received and consequently aims to conserve or preserve those blessings.”

John R. Puri is the Thomas L. Rhodes Fellow at National Review.

#5943. Thrifty Traveler Is 30% Off For Black Friday—A Year Of Flight And Business Class Award Alerts For $90.99

They tell me this is their biggest sale of the year, and the biggest they expect to offer for the foreseeable future. It matches the 30% discount I covered in August.

Readers who took advantage of the offer before their March price increase did better: $79 for the first year and $99 for renewals. That offer’s gone. The regular annual prices are now $129.99 and $189.99, and their price lock guarantee applies to those full prices, not the discounted first year.

I’ve said this is one of the better services for finding rare premium cabin awards. They search departures from more than 200 airports in the U.S. and Canada, and you choose which airports you want alerts for. You can stick to your home airport or include other cities you’re willing to position to.

Deals arrive by email, there’s an online hub where you can browse them, and you can opt into text alerts for mistake fares and their rarest “unicorn” deals. They say they’ve recently sent more than 80 flight alerts in a month, including more than 30 business class award alerts, such as:

Most alerts won’t fit any one person’s plans. I like this most for someone with transferable points who can let award availability help decide where to go. Finding one useful business class award can easily justify the subscription. If you need a particular flight on a particular date, though, a stream of deals to other places isn’t going to solve that.

They’ve also added FareTracker. Premium members can track up to 10 cash flights and get an email when the price drops by at least $20, with instructions to rebook and claim the difference as an airline credit. You still need a fare whose rules allow that, and you have to do the rebooking. But it’s a useful reason to keep watching a ticket after you’ve bought it.

The Premium+ bundle adds hotel deals, including difficult award availability and discounted paid stays. Recent alerts have included Park Hyatt Kyoto and the renovated Waldorf Astoria New York. The extra $42 makes sense if you’d build a trip around finding award nights at a property like that.

#5941. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are important rules to know.

The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

“It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

Read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

Most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

That means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

If you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

Other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

With many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”

TSA officers have historically said that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

If your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

Every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

Whether you plan to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

#5937. What Is the Fantasy in Grand Theft Auto Really All About?

Gamers play Grand Theft Auto VI on the game’s release day at Bamboo Gaming Center in Bangkok, Thailand, November 19, 2026.

I will not be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. The limited flexibility left in my wrists after decades of typing and mousing and gaming must be reserved for a game I started three years ago and haven’t finished. I’m stuck in a shed in the rain, low on ammo, and there is a big Nazi robot outside. I have to find the time and desire to return to this dangerous situation and beat the robot before the red bar over my head that reads CARPAL TUNNEL goes fully red. But the main reason I won’t play GTA: I don’t wish to inhabit the life of an uninhibited sociopath.

Nor do I need a girlfriend. Rob Henderson, in The Spectator, notes:

#5936. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images)

That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

“It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

“I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

“You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”

Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

“This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”

Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”

“The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”

Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

“I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

“I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

“Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”

On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

“You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”

John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is a great choice for beginners and experienced points-and-miles enthusiasts who want an easy way to earn miles — all for an affordable $95 annual fee.

The Venture Rewards card's current welcome offer is especially compelling — but this is your last chance to take advantage of it.

You can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, you'll receive a $300 credit upon approval to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year.

Here's what the offer is worth and what to know before applying.

Apply now for a limited-time offer on the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn more than $1,000 in travel bonuses with a limited-time $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, plus earn 75,000 bonus miles once you spend $4,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening.

New Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, you'll receive a $300 credit upon approval to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year. This offer ends soon.

Including the credit, this offer is worth $1,688, per TPG’s November 2026 valuations.

In terms of miles alone, this is the standard welcome bonus on the card. However, the inclusion of the $300 credit makes this offer among the most valuable we've seen.

For comparison, previous welcome offers have gone as high as 100,000 miles after meeting the minimum spending requirements (no longer available), but with no credit.

It’s possible to squeeze even more from that bonus if you redeem Capital One miles for maximum value, thanks to their impressive roster of 15-plus transfer partners.

There are some eligibility requirements to keep in mind before applying. You don't want to waste a hard pull on your credit report if you aren't eligible for the current offer.

First, if you've previously earned a welcome bonus on the Venture Rewards, you won't be able to earn another one for 48 months. Note that this is 48 months from the date you received your bonus, not from the date you were approved.

In addition, if you previously earned a welcome bonus on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, you will more than likely not be eligible to earn a welcome bonus on the Venture Rewards.

Capital One may consider multiple factors when deciding whether to approve you; for a deeper dive into its application requirements, check out our full guide.

Related: The best Capital One credit cards

This card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases. So, by spending $4,000 on it to earn the welcome bonus, you’d earn at least 83,000 miles in the first few months, including the welcome bonus.

And since the Venture Rewards earns 5 miles per dollar spent on car rentals, hotels and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel, it’s possible to earn even more miles while working toward your welcome bonus.

While some travel credit cards may earn slightly higher rates on select categories such as groceries or dining, the draw here is the simplicity and guarantee of earning at least 2 miles per dollar spent on anything you buy without the need to memorize multiple bonus spending categories.

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

Your total value from this welcome bonus depends largely on how you redeem your miles. There are two key options:

When converting your miles to hotel points or airline miles, most partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, though a couple of partners have different ratios. You can get great sweet spot redemptions by transferring miles to programs like Air Canada Aeroplan and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

For example, TPG's editor-in-chief, Nick Ewen, transferred 117,000 Capital One miles to Emirates Skywards to upgrade himself and two family members to Emirates first class. This broke down to 39,000 miles per person, a reasonable cost for the upgrade.

If you don’t want to transfer your miles, you can redeem them by booking a trip through Capital One Travel. These redemptions can be very handy in a world where you may be renting recreational vehicles, booking vacation home rentals or securing a cabin close to home more often than hopping on a flight to the other side of the world.

Related: Cashing in Capital One miles? How to get the maximum value when redeeming miles

The Capital One Venture Rewards doesn’t offer the same benefits as more premium travel rewards cards, including its upscale sibling, the Capital One Venture X Rewards.

But for its modest $95 annual fee, the Venture Rewards provides some useful benefits:

Related: Chase Sapphire Preferred Card vs. Capital One Venture Rewards

The Capital One Venture Rewards remains a strong option for travelers who value simplicity. It earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases and gives cardholders access to Capital One's airline and hotel transfer partners, all for a $95 annual fee.

Plus, the current welcome offer — which ends soon — includes a solid haul of miles and a $300 credit for Capital One Travel, one of the best offers we've seen. Just remember to use your credit in the first cardholder year, or you'll forfeit the value.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture Rewards.

#5933. Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough. Being told the airport protects you from excessive prices, while it approves the price and collects money from the shop, is actually worse. There’s a new, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match. Airports usually defended the prices. I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement. Those are the reasons we get both the pricing promises and the prices that don’t match. Airports make concessions expensive to operate, then collect money from businesses selling to passengers who have limited alternatives. The starting point is understanding that passengers aren’t the customer, they’re the product. The Airport Sells Access To You An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same company with products sourced from the same vendor. And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too. Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget showed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants. I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops. Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive said the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years. Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Street Pricing Depends On Which Street You Choose Many airports promise that vendors will charge the same prices as comparable businesses outside the airport, or those prices plus an allowed premium. The airport industry’s 2025 concessions survey found street pricing plus a percentage at 80% of responding large hubs. Chicago’s sample concession agreement calls for value pricing tied to approved off-airport stores, without a general percentage premium. The Port Authority Of New York New Jersey’s manual uses three to six approved comparison locations. Branded restaurants and shops generally must be compared with locations of the same brand. In the video, the Port Authority defends a $6.89 bottle of water by saying Hudson is a specialty market rather than a bodega. That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Shows The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! When consumers face high prices. Topics on this pageAirportConcessionPrice gougingRetailChicagoDallas Fort Worth International AirportDenverHudson GroupJohn F. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! Kennedy International AirportLas VegasLos AngelesMinneapolisNew JerseyPhoenixPort Authority of New York and New JerseyPortlandSalt Lake CityStarbucksUnited Airlines+15 more More From View from the Wing

An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same company with products sourced from the same vendor.

And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too.

Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget showed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants.

I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops.

Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive said the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years.

Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Street Pricing Depends On Which Street You Choose Many airports promise that vendors will charge the same prices as comparable businesses outside the airport, or those prices plus an allowed premium. The airport industry’s 2025 concessions survey found street pricing plus a percentage at 80% of responding large hubs. Chicago’s sample concession agreement calls for value pricing tied to approved off-airport stores, without a general percentage premium. The Port Authority Of New York New Jersey’s manual uses three to six approved comparison locations. Branded restaurants and shops generally must be compared with locations of the same brand. In the video, the Port Authority defends a $6.89 bottle of water by saying Hudson is a specialty market rather than a bodega. That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Shows The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. A good explanation but the MSP fee was removed in 2025.

The irony is that the vast majority of the elite buy nothing at airports. Almost all my food and drink needs are met by the lounges and Priority Pass restaurants, and only a fool goes shopping at an airport. So I don’t care what political nonsense goes on with the restaurants and shops. If I happen to be visiting a non-lounge airport, I just take basic steps to prepare for that. Like I have an empty water bottle with me.

You make a strong case for why vendor pricing at airports is elevated when compared to shops outside of an airport. It’s always best to avoid shopping at airports for these reasons. Of course, sometimes it can not be avoided, but even then one should attempt to minimize one’s purchases.

Let’s not forget the excessive profits flowing to the handful of airport concession operators that dominate both in the US and Europe.

I have been boycotting all purchases in the airport concourses as the prices are obscene. If there was a major increase in the number of persons also boycotting, then perhaps there will be some recognition of the price-gouging being endorsed by airport governments. The whole pricing system for air travel and ancillaries needs to be scrutinized and appropriate corrective measures taken. I tend to remember when railroads were the major passenger provider and there were price limits. Also the ancillary services in the train stations had prices very close to what you would pay if you left the station and walked across the street to make the same purchase.

Well, Gary, this piece truly explains why much time here is spent on talking about lounges. If you have access to a lounge, don’t kvetch about the shops and restaurants. And if you are not a member, make or buy some sammies before you get to the airport, and eat them at the boarding area. And bring an empty water bottle and fill it up after clearing security.

#5932. Will America Finally Confront the Massive Chinese Espionage Threat?

The Jensen Huang saga shows us that China’s spying is aggressive and ubiquitous.

Then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a keynote speech at Computex in Taipei, Taiwan, May 19, 2025.

Every few months, Washington rediscovers that China is spying on Americans en masse, expresses shock, and goes back to business as usual. And once again, it has happened. As a nation, we need to learn that our primary adversary is highly capable, extremely aggressive, and never lets morals or principles stand in its way. In other words, we must take the challenge posed by Chinese intelligence, cybersecurity, and influence seriously and protect ourselves accordingly.

According to widespread reporting this fall, U.S. intelligence concluded that a Chinese businesswoman who befriended Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, while her company bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia AI chips was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Her Singapore-based firm reportedly began a multibillion-dollar purchase of Nvidia chips shortly after she was first photographed with Huang publicly. Her husband, Kang Wei, who originally introduced his wife to the Nvidia CEO, has in recent years built a massive data center empire with the overt support of the Chinese government. Of course, Nvidia says it complies with the law and has opened an internal investigation into the relationship. Beijing says that any claims about espionage are smears, as it always does. Huang, who had hidden this and other affairs from his board and colleagues, has resigned in disgrace but is now reported to be planning a comeback.

Then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a keynote speech at Computex in Taipei, Taiwan, May 19, 2025.

Gregory W. Slayton is a former senior U.S. diplomat, chairman of Slayton Capital, and author of Portraits of Ukraine: A Nation at War.

On “Will America Finally Confront the Massive Chinese Espionage Threat?”

#5931. The House has a new lame-duck challenge: Attendance

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a new challenge: Attendance.

Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

"Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members."

“We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

“I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”

And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

“There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

“I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”

Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

“The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”
