#5919. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

#5918. Delta Flight Attendants May Get Their First Union Vote Since 2010 — But Saying Yes Could Mean Smaller Paychecks

Delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play. It can be a useful stalking horse, where the airline pays up generously to keep its crew from unionizing. But once they actually pull the trigger, there’s little reason – or ability – to continue paying above industry wages. AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson says she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines. Brian Sumers came away from their November 12 interview at the Skift Aviation Forum thinking she’ll get an election and win it. A vote in 2027 is a real possibility. If I were Delta crew I’d vote no. The union would get about 30,000 flight attendants to represent. Crews who already get better than what other airline unions bargain for could wind up taking home less. Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%. The National Mediation Board needs valid cards from at least half the eligible flight attendants, and a card more than a year old won’t count. Delta organizers put the minimum at roughly 15,000 signatures. Once there’s an election, a majority of valid votes cast decides it. Nelson also said she was months away in 2024. Later that November organizers said they were weeks from having the cards. Delta flight attendants have rejected representation three times, but the vote after the Northwest merger was close. In 2010, 9,544 voted against representation and 9,216 voted for it. Sumers says he hears more confidence from Nelson this time. She can pick when to file, and a loss would normally mean waiting a year to try again while cards expire. If Nelson files with a comfortable cushion above the threshold, that would give her the edge in an election. Delta’s Pay Advantage Is Profit Sharing American Airlines and United Airlines now pay slightly higher hourly rates at the top of the flight pay scale. It’s $86.32 per flight hour at Delta, $87.04 at American and $87.47 at United. At 80 flight hours a month, United’s $1.15 advantage is about $1,100 a year in base pay.For newer hires, Delta starts a little higher than both. But Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year. Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a new hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026. United got boarding pay in its new deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. . The Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants. Union Flight Attendants Go A Long Time Between Raises Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the new contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. The National Mediation Board can release the parties from mediation, normally starting a 30 day cooling off period before the union can strike or the airline can impose new terms. In practice that hasn’t happened for flight attendants since 1993. Nelson said at Skift that she wants more frequent bargaining to deliver smaller, more regular raises. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers. American Airlines and United Airlines now pay slightly higher hourly rates at the top of the flight pay scale. It’s $86.32 per flight hour at Delta, $87.04 at American and $87.47 at United. At 80 flight hours a month, United’s $1.15 advantage is about $1,100 a year in base pay.For newer hires, Delta starts a little higher than both.

But Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year.

Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a new hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026.

United got boarding pay in its new deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. .

The Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants.

Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the new contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed).

To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election.

Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement.

At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers.

1) Using 80 hrs per month to compare flight attendants’ pay is not realistic. Most flight attendants can knock out 80 hours of flying in 10 days worked or less, so many will work 150-160 hour months instead. Besides, even at the top of United’s flight attendant pay scale ($87.47/hr, 12th year, according to this articls) good luck living near some of the most expensive places in the US, or commuting to them several times a month and needing accommodations there (crash pad, transportation, meals on the road, and/or hotels on your own) to get to and from work on under $7,000 per month before paying a single penny in taxes, FICA, health care, social security, etc. because you only work 80 hours.

Therefore, the difference between a realistic United/American vs. Delta flight attendant “salary” is probably closer to double what this article estimated.

2) Union contracts are not only about the pay rates. That’s why it’s only one section of about 25 or so. ALL the rest is SO vital to job and career protections. They codify everything about how the company can treat you at work, and the vast majority of the time THEY are the reasons a work group considers union representation. It’s not the Shiny Pay Rates. It’s the work rules.

3) Delta has spend a TON of energy, and even money, keeping union representation off the property with their flight attendants. If you think they increase pay, or give boarding pay 1st, or offer generous profit sharing because management is just nice – come and see my bridge for sale. That would be a violation of their fiduciary duty to shareholders, anyhow.

No, they do it because it would cost more to have a unionized workforce. Delta wants to keep saving money by keeping the flight attendants non-union. They want the financial advantage that comes with it.

@Pilot Paul – as I write, unionization is a strong card to have but not play. Actually playing it imposes costs on Delta that ultimately come out of pay. But the threat keeps flight attendants at the top of the pay scale, and they don’t have to remit dues for it either.

But for Delta it’s not just about ‘saving money’ – it’s about keeping the service culture that helps drive a revenue premium. Delta flight attendants are friendlier than American’s and United’s!

Disagreed, @Pilot Paul. Regarding your first statement and using your math, the article estimated $ 1100 per year in pay differential (based on 80 hour months). Even if it doubled (based on 160 hour months), that would add only $ 1100 more. Meanwhile, Delta points out that the Profit Sharing alone is worth $ 5100 to $ 6200 a year, which makes your “doubling” worth only 20 % (or less) of the Profit Sharing. Regarding your statement #2, you are right that “Union contracts are not only about the pay rates”. Essentially, you’re proving the point that main attraction of Unions to some workforces is that the employees can work less (or conform to company rules and guidelines less) because they’ll be protected by the Union. Which destroys your Point #3: Delta (like many other corporations), strongly prefers NOT to have a Union as they ultimately end up with a lower quality workforce who will not provide the Brand Promise which they wish to convey. It’s NOT about cost savings at all. As for Delta being the 1st to offer Boarding Pay and the only Airline to offer significant Profit Sharing, they didn’t “do it because it would cost more to have a unionized workforce”, they paid more because they value their workforce and see it as win-win for them AND their employees to keep it non-union.

Gary, not contradicting that unionization is a strong card to play. The threat of voting to bring in the union IS actually very good leverage, and probably the one thing that actually has improved the Delta flight attendant compensation over the years (as opposed to just management benevolence). But in my experience, even union members often don’t look past the pay scales when considering whether a contract is good or not. As someone who’s worked at both union and non-union locations, there’s so much more to consider. And it’s often worth being “officially union” for that part of the job, even if the bottom-line pay works out slightly smaller. Let’s talk scope some day, and the number of mainline jobs at pretty much every carrier it has created (well, except at Southwest).

I do disagree with you Delta’s motivations, however – I do believe it’s all about saving money for them, rather than the culture. And I also believe unionization doesn’t automatically spoil a culture. What I’ve witnessed more often that does ruin it is a toxic management, regardless of whether there is union representation or not.

None the less, thanks for writing about this. It will be interesting to watch what happens.

>>> “2, you are right that “Union contracts are not only about the pay rates”. Essentially, you’re proving the point that main attraction of Unions to some workforces is that the employees can work less (or conform to company rules and guidelines less) because they’ll be protected by the Union.”

No, that’s not true. It’s not about “working less” or getting protected by the union. It’s about a balance to create reasonable work rules in a demanding career. But here’s a specific example: Delta flight attendants can, and will, work Continuous Duty Overnights. Their work rules allow, and the company regularly schedules, trips where the flight attendants are “on duty” at the hotel. What does this mean?

Normally, a crew needs a minimum amount of rest – codified both by federal rules AND the union contract. But airlines can get around that by having you come “on duty” at 9pm and staying on duty until 9am. You get scheduled to arrive at the outstation at 11:45pm… get to the hotel at 12:45am, and in your room at 1am. And you have a 4:45 van for your 6am departure the next morning. Enjoy your 3 hours sleep!

And that’s IF you are on-time. If you are late, the morning departure does not have to be delayed – you are on a legal duty overnight and now you just get 1-2 hours of “sleep” and then are expected to soldier on.

Union contracts will have rules against onerous scheduling like this example. THAT is the type of stuff a union contract can implement – it’s not about “working less” but rather about not getting abused by a management that is interested in staffing all the flights at the lowest possible cost.

And – yes, if profit sharing stays high, airlines with generous profit sharing will pay more to workers over the whole year. But it’s a double-edged sword. When times are tough, and the airline doesn’t make as much (typically in an economic downturn) – down goes your pay too. It’s like having a low base salary with high commissions. Make lots of sales – things are great! Make very few, not so good. And depending on profit sharing is depending on something outside of your control.

I like high profit sharing – but not at the expense of “that’s why we keep your salary below your peers” logic.

Sara Nelson needs to go back to the line. She merely wants more union dues which will bring her a bigger salary. Delta has a better culture than every other airline out there. Start unionizing the rest of the groups and watch them turn into UAL or AAL

Unless the flight attendant population has really changed in the last few years, therebl is no way the union will win the vote.

I wonder how much pay Delta flight attendants lose by not having pay protection, sick pay etc today that Gary has ignored. There’s more than just hourly pay in these contracts Gary. Maybe you should calculate that before saying these guys are winning so hard.

Then you have all of those being fired for minimal reasons etc on top so they have less job security as well compared to those at AA.

DL’s founding CEO believed firmly that if you take care of your employees, they will take care of your customers.

DL has consistently delivered better service while paying its people more. And it has nothing to do with union vs. non-union. DL’s unionized pilots are better compensated than any other US airline pilot group precisely because of the same profit sharing that helps DL FAs. It took DL pilots to come up w/ an agreement w/ DL that DOUBLED what UA offered its pilots and its pilots wisely voted down.

and in this whole discussion, it has yet to be shown that Sara Nelson has been saying for years that she will unionize DL FAs. Even if she gets to 50% of cards does not mean she will get 50% votes. DL FAs know what is at stake and are happy to threaten unionization in order for DL to sweeten the pot even while knowing that actually voting for a union will cost them.

DL employees watched the 5 years it took UA to settle with its FAs even as their purchasing power SHRUNK in a period of the highest inflation they will see in their lifetime; in the same period, DL employees got multiple payraises and profit sharing that is larger than the entire rest of the US airline industry COMBINED.

how can some people be so consistently wrong and yet just double down on banging the keyboard to argue against what everyone else can see?

@Miles Waren Rich – ~ 1/3 of Delta’s flight attendants joined since the pandemic ~ half joined since the last union election in 2010.

I have not read the article but Democrat or Republican… this congressional piece of crap should never be allowed into office

There are so many congress people who are not only delinquent with their Federal Taxes, have questionable citizenship or loyalty to our country, or are just downright sketchy that it sickens me.

Do you ever feel your grandchildren or children are doomed too?

Those 80 hours are hours in the air. Sorry Pilot Paul, no one is doing 160 willingly. My wife is top 3% in seniority at a US airline and flies 50-75 hours monthly because she enjoys a higher quality of life and more vacation travel.

It has been a messy few weeks for air travel in the U.S. Unfortunately, it appears the Thanksgiving rush could bring another big wave of flight delays.

Storm systems developing along both coasts threaten to disrupt holiday plans for travelers catching last-minute flights.

On the West Coast, United Airlines is letting flyers passing through its San Francisco International Airport (SFO) hub change their tickets as heavy rain and wind move into the Bay Area, coinciding with the travel rush.

Meanwhile, forecasters are warning of a “monster” storm that could disrupt flights at several of the nation’s busiest East Coast hubs on Wednesday and Thursday.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen told TPG.

It’s looking like the latest in a series of frustrations for flyers. In the past two weeks alone, travelers dealt with a nationwide ground stop that led to 18,000 flight cancellations as well as technology outages at United and Delta Air Lines.

Now, it appears Mother Nature will be the biggest obstacle during one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

The West Coast storm is expected to impact the Thanksgiving getaway.

Late Monday, United issued a travel advisory for its San Francisco hub — a sign the carrier expects disruptions on the eve of Thanksgiving.

Fortunately, Bay Area leaders appear less worried about flooding at the airport itself.

In recent days, forecasters had grown concerned that heavy rain and high tides could lead to water covering SFO’s taxiways, which are right next to San Francisco Bay.

“At this moment, we are not expecting flood water to reach onto the tarmac at SFO, which is a positive development,” San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media post — while warning that ground stops because of weather conditions were “still a possibility.”

In a statement to TPG, SFO officials said the airport was keeping pump stations and drainage areas clear, and staging sandbags ahead of the forecasted bad weather.

The worst travel disruptions could come from a powerful coastal storm developing in the east, meteorologists warn.

That East Coast system could bring strong winds, heavy rain and flooding to a large swath of the coast — including many of the nation’s busiest airports, according to Van Dillen.

He laid out which airports could be heavily affected:

“My advice would be, the earlier you can get to your destination, the better,” Van Dillen advised East Coast travelers.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself is typically one of the quietest days of the year at airports.

All eyes will be on how Mother Nature cooperates on Sunday, as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

More 2026 Thanksgiving travel coverage from TPG:

Here are some things you should do if you're planning to fly in the next few days.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: as more and more cities are affected by bad weather, it’s likely the disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#5915. Woman Faced A Felony Charge For Stealing A Rental Car—Then Won A Seat In Congress And Prosecutors Dropped The Case

This year was such a wave election that in some cases candidate quality didn’t matter at all. It was enough to win just not to be a Republican. Shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally. A sheriff’s deputy pulled up behind her. He handed her a felony summons for stealing a Toyota Corolla she’d rented from Budget nearly seven years earlier. The incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad. She won anyway. And on Tuesday, after Budget got paid for the six weeks its car was overdue, the district attorney dropped the charge for good. It’s good to get elected to Congress. Budget Car Rental Got The Corolla Back In 2019 Womack picked up the car in Charlotte on August 27, 2019, and renewed the rental twice. Her last extension began October 7, 2019. According to the police report the vehicle was due back at noon on October 23. On November 26 an officer reported that police couldn’t find her and put out an all points bulletin. Police recovered the Corolla and returned it to Budget on December 4, 42 days late. Budget sold the vehicle the following year. Womack has a number of excuses for never returning the car. She says a diabetic seizure and long hospitalization had wiped her out financially. (It’s not clear why that kept her from returning it.) Her son went into foster care while she was in the hospital (again, unclear why that kept her from returning it) and the two of them wound up living in a hotel (hotels have parking, but the hotel didn’t force her to keep the car). She’d expected the company to come get the car. She says she had nowhere reliable to receive mail (when you rent a car you know you’re supposed to give it back, even without a mailed notice) and she thought the matter was settled (exactly how it would have been is unclear). On January 14, 2020, a court issued a summons for felony failure to return the car. Under North Carolina law, willfully keeping a rental vehicle past its deadline is a felony if the vehicle is worth more than $4,000. The car was valued at $20,000. Womack says she first heard about the case on Friday, October 9, 2026. A local reporter posted the records. She responded, “I do owe them people some money, obviously.” BREAKING: Documents pulled from the NC Courts government website show District 14 congressional candidate Lakesha Womack has a “pending” felony warrant for failure to return a rental car in 2019. Police records say Budget Car Rental rented a car to Womack on Oct. 7, 2019 and it was supposed be returned on Oct 23, 2019. Pics and links attached. https://t.co/4WZRvweFxM — Brett Jensen WBT News (@Brett_Jensen) October 9, 2026 Two days later, on October 11, the summons was reissued. A Polk County deputy’s body camera caught the handoff outside the county Democratic rally. Republican Congressman Tim Moore ran an ad on this. Watch Tim Moore’s campaign ad, “Keep Your Money.” He Helped Draw The District. She Didn’t Even Live In It. Moore spent ten years as speaker of the North Carolina House, helped gerrymander the district to favor Republicans and won it in 2024 by nearly 65,000 votes. Womack, an ordained minister making her first run for public office, lived in a neighboring district and said she had no plans to move. A House member only has to live in the state. Through October 14, Moore had spent $1,921,880 to Womack’s $55,626. He spent nearly $1 million on ads. She had no paid full-time staff and didn’t buy a TV spot. Three days after the deputy served her she was handing out T-shirts to striking workers at Charlotte Douglas airport. Moore won five of the six counties. He even won the Election Day vote by 21,246. But early in-person voting, which started four days after the deputy showed up, gave Womack a 24,700 vote lead. With the felony case still pending, she posted, “#HatersGonnaHate I’m still Congresswoman-Elect.” On November 16 prosecutors learned she’d reached a deal with Budget. She paid the assessed rental cost for the overdue period. Budget told prosecutors it was satisfied. Campaign donations may not have mattered in the race, but that’s an unusually inexpensive way to buy goodwill with a member of the U.S. House of Representatives. On November 24 the state dismissed the charge with prejudice. This Wasn’t Hertz When I first wrote about Womack on October 11, my entire comment was “Ruh roh – it wasn’t Hertz.” A reader guessed Budget had lost track of a car it already had back. A father and his 13-year-old daughter were held at gunpoint outside Savannah in a car they’d just rented from Hertz’s Thrifty brand. When police let the father show them his rental agreement, it was 36 minutes old. The car had been reported stolen before Thrifty handed him the keys. A Hertz President’s Circle member wound up in jail over a Salt Lake City rental he’d extended, returned and paid $3,900 for. Those arrest stories seemed to dry up after Hertz brought in Palantir to help track its fleet in 2022 and agreed to pay $168 million to settle 364 claims. At Least Womack Was Still Campaigning North Carolina Republicans drew a map they expected would give them 11 of the state’s 14 U.S. House seats. Democrats won 11. Elsewhere the wave carried a couple of candidates who’d actually stopped campaigning. In Iowa, Eric Armstrong suspended his state House campaign on September 7 for health reasons. He beat a county supervisor and retired police lieutenant by about ten points. In Texas, Ericka Lomick suspended her campaign when a federal mortgage fraud conviction raised questions about whether she could serve. Her name stayed on the ballot for both the rest of the outgoing state representative’s term and the next one. She beat the same Republican in both elections. He’s asked the Texas Supreme Court to block certification of the special election. In California, Womack’s $55,626 would’ve looked like a fortune to Hipolito Cerros. The 28-year-old former mayor raised no campaign money, hired no staff and bought no ads. He unseated the Republican leader of the state Assembly. Tennessee tech support worker Victoria Broderick lost to Congressman Scott DesJarlais in 2024. He took 70% of the vote. After Republicans redrew the district, she ran again. She was still working full time and had to message her boss the morning after the election. The race was called for her the same day Womack’s charge was dropped. My personal favorite this cycle is Maricopa County, Arizona’s Sebastian Matta – a 19-year-old Arizona State philosophy sophomore – who beat a former state senator to become clerk of the Superior Court. He’d filed his campaign finance paperwork late and blamed his accountant for going quiet on him. He’ll run an office that processes 15,000 documents a day. To rent a Corolla from Budget at the Phoenix airport, he’s still two years short of the usual minimum age. In 2012, the anti-gay Democrat running as the incumbent for state representative in Hutchinson, Kanasa defeated her primary challenger – an openly gay son of a former member of the Ku Klux Klan – and then went on to best her Republican opponent who was a pro-gay rights, pro-choice train conductor named Dakota Bass. That race was featured in season two, episode eight of The Newsroom. (HT: Paul H.) When police let the father show them his rental agreement, it was 36 minutes old. The car had been reported stolen before Thrifty handed him the keys. A Hertz President’s Circle member wound up in jail over a Salt Lake City rental he’d extended, returned and paid $3,900 for. Those arrest stories seemed to dry up after Hertz brought in Palantir to help track its fleet in 2022 and agreed to pay $168 million to settle 364 claims. At Least Womack Was Still Campaigning North Carolina Republicans drew a map they expected would give them 11 of the state’s 14 U.S. House seats. Democrats won 11. Elsewhere the wave carried a couple of candidates who’d actually stopped campaigning. In Iowa, Eric Armstrong suspended his state House campaign on September 7 for health reasons. He beat a county supervisor and retired police lieutenant by about ten points. In Texas, Ericka Lomick suspended her campaign when a federal mortgage fraud conviction raised questions about whether she could serve. Her name stayed on the ballot for both the rest of the outgoing state representative’s term and the next one. She beat the same Republican in both elections. He’s asked the Texas Supreme Court to block certification of the special election. In California, Womack’s $55,626 would’ve looked like a fortune to Hipolito Cerros. The 28-year-old former mayor raised no campaign money, hired no staff and bought no ads. He unseated the Republican leader of the state Assembly. Tennessee tech support worker Victoria Broderick lost to Congressman Scott DesJarlais in 2024. He took 70% of the vote. After Republicans redrew the district, she ran again. She was still working full time and had to message her boss the morning after the election. The race was called for her the same day Womack’s charge was dropped. My personal favorite this cycle is Maricopa County, Arizona’s Sebastian Matta – a 19-year-old Arizona State philosophy sophomore – who beat a former state senator to become clerk of the Superior Court. He’d filed his campaign finance paperwork late and blamed his accountant for going quiet on him. He’ll run an office that processes 15,000 documents a day. To rent a Corolla from Budget at the Phoenix airport, he’s still two years short of the usual minimum age. In 2012, the anti-gay Democrat running as the incumbent for state representative in Hutchinson, Kanasa defeated her primary challenger – an openly gay son of a former member of the Ku Klux Klan – and then went on to best her Republican opponent who was a pro-gay rights, pro-choice train conductor named Dakota Bass. That race was featured in season two, episode eight of The Newsroom. (HT: Paul H.) Moore spent ten years as speaker of the North Carolina House, helped gerrymander the district to favor Republicans and won it in 2024 by nearly 65,000 votes.

Womack, an ordained minister making her first run for public office, lived in a neighboring district and said she had no plans to move. A House member only has to live in the state.

Through October 14, Moore had spent $1,921,880 to Womack’s $55,626. He spent nearly $1 million on ads. She had no paid full-time staff and didn’t buy a TV spot.

Three days after the deputy served her she was handing out T-shirts to striking workers at Charlotte Douglas airport.

Moore won five of the six counties. He even won the Election Day vote by 21,246. But early in-person voting, which started four days after the deputy showed up, gave Womack a 24,700 vote lead.

With the felony case still pending, she posted, “#HatersGonnaHate I’m still Congresswoman-Elect.”

On November 16 prosecutors learned she’d reached a deal with Budget. She paid the assessed rental cost for the overdue period. Budget told prosecutors it was satisfied. Campaign donations may not have mattered in the race, but that’s an unusually inexpensive way to buy goodwill with a member of the U.S. House of Representatives. On November 24 the state dismissed the charge with prejudice.

The poor people of NC, having this criminal “representing” them.

Summarizing: – Woman didn’t return rental car as per her contract. (Theft? Conversion? Breach of contract? The first two are criminal.) – Prosecutor drops carges [coincidentally?] once she’s elected – Woman shows no remorse

I’m confident if I got the summary wrong someone will correct me.

#1: I’m going for Theft as a minimum, police report justified, and prosecutor charges as well. Later had her attitude been better than “well maybe I should have returned THEIR car” (paraphrased) maybe walk it down to breach of contract or misunderstanding.

#2: Her getting elected changes no facts on the ground. She rented a car. She signed a rental contract. She failed to abide by it, and “kept the car” beyond her right to keep that car. The prosecutor rightly carged her, but the story doesnt seem to indicate WHICH charges were filed? And yet once elected the prosecutor dropped the charges. Why? (that’s a whole lot of question involving a who, a why, and a why now and not before or after.)

Is this justice? I I rent a car and don’t return it and the cops stop me I should be overjoyed to stay alive. Apparently she’s in a “better class of people” who can jocularly opine that maybe she should have returned the car.

I don’t know whom she represents, but I didn’t vote for her, and wouldn’t.

WAIT! So she’s actually a case where the person DID steal the car, and THIS is the time the rental car company decides to drop it.

I’m here for the comments defending her keeping the car.

Hmmmm . . . sitting on this for 7 years AFTER they recovered the car. I’m sure this is entirely coincidental and had nothing to do with the election. This is one of the clearest cases of a simple civil matter at this point for monetary damages. No chance in hell there wasn’t some political instigation to any criminal charges suddenly becoming alive again nearly 7 years after they got the car back.

@David – the felony summons was issued six years ago. The felony wasn’t invented because she was running for Congress. She stole a car!

Keeping the car, or simply failing to return the car for a while?

This looks like the latter. A whole bunch of problems, returning the car wasn’t high on her priorities. It was returned, I do not see criminal **intent**, I see someone overwhelmed. I doubt I would vote guilty, but I doubt I would vote for her in the election. This was not exactly good judgment.

Bold decision-makers that aren’t afraid of taking risks tend to make great leaders.

She is likely a one term event and will draw a primary opponent next cycle It was a yellow dog election — people voted for anything that was not an R.

Shit happens. When shit happens to poor people, it happens a lot worse.

Now, do I know that her excuses are legit or not? I do not. But in our country, if you are living paycheck to paycheck like most American workers, and you get sick, and you are hospitalized, you lose everything, and you have to prioritize, and maybe not returning a rental car is your least bad choice of all your bad choices – especially if you were hospitalized for something as simple as not being able to afford your insulin.

Is that what happened? No idea. Is that would could have happened? Is our healthcare “system” destroying the lives of hundreds of thousands of WORKING Americans each year a thing? Yes it is.

Run a company that steals millions from their customers with fake fees or signing you up for fake accounts and you get to force your customers into individual binding arbitration if they want it back. Keep a rental car too long and we jump to throwing that person in prison for years.

Also, is the North Carolina law REALLY that keeping a car past the return deadline is a felony? Surely there’s more to it than that? I did that last month when I postponed my flight a day. Hertz added a day to my bill.

Lastly, if this were a random white man, nobody would bat an eye if a rental car company accepted payment of the past-due balance over charging them with a felony. Most of you are only mad because of the picture.

Lock her up!!! Lock her up!!! Lock her up!!!

Borrowing with no intention of ever giving it back? She’s a perfect fit for any Congress!

#5914. At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

“I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” said Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

“I respect them,” he said. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”

Peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”

Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

#INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

New leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

The last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

#5913. It Takes a Family

The answers aren’t political and institutional; they are deeply relational.

John Mulaney in Saturday Night Live’s “Sister” sketch

The recent Saturday Night Live “Sister” skit hit a nerve with its fake ad for a 24-hour elder-care service. The service is “completely free,” provided you’re the brother.

“My dad means the world to me,” it begins, with comedian John Mulaney narrating. “So, when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible. I didn’t want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn’t know where to turn.”

This is one of the best times of the year to find flight deals. Black Friday is almost here, followed quickly by Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday. All the major airlines, hotels and booking platforms have big sales. Of course, TPG will have roundups of all the best deals, but there are other ways to find deals that I've been experimenting with: artificial intelligence.

I've been an AI skeptic the past few years, at least when it comes to finding and booking travel deals, but it has come a long way since TPG tried to use AI to plan an itinerary back in 2023. (Spoiler: It didn't do a great job.)

But the technology has improved significantly over the past few years, especially when it comes to confirming you are getting a good deal.

ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and Google Gemini can now also help you compare prices and find cheaper airports or travel dates, decipher fare rules and restrictions, and even let you know whether it's better to pay cash or use points or miles.

I still don't find AI great at finding mileage or points awards, but it can do a lot.

"AI is already a powerful tool for finding flight deals and only getting better, but it’s still got a long way to go," Thrifty Traveler executive editor Kyle Potter said. "It’s prone to mistakes and falls victim to phantom award availability."

Still, combining AI with tools like Google Flights and Points Path can make finding deals easier and potentially save you some serious money (or miles).

So it can be a useful tool, but I don’t think it’ll ever be the only tool travelers need.

Here are some ways to use AI to find deals.

Like I always tell people looking for deals, flexibility is key. Rather than asking for a specific date or flight, describe your budget, home airport, ideal travel dates and how flexible you are in your AI tool.

AI will work with tools like Google Flights to help you find a good deal. Here's a sample prompt:

"I'm looking for Black Friday flight deals departing from New York City. My budget is $500 round-trip, I'm flexible on destinations, and I can travel between January and March 2027. Suggest 10 destinations worth checking, including nearby airports and typical fare ranges. Don't invent live prices."

ChatGPT gave me a list of potential deals.

It also showed some of its top picks, including San Juan and Barcelona.

As I continued scrolling, ChatGPT eventually showed me a link to Google Flights Explore, one of my absolute favorite tools for finding flight deals. As you can see, this prompt pulls up a Google Flights search for some cheap trips from New York City-area airports to places nearby and, if you scroll the map, far away, too. I had to narrow the search a bit for just trips in January, but there were a ton of options.

You may be asking yourself why you need AI if you are going to Google Flights Explore anyway. Great point — I think the idea is that ChatGPT can give you a few ideas tailored to your specific interests and budget.

AI can also help you find savings by flying into cheaper airports or on different travel dates that will save you some cash. You might try Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) instead of San Francisco International Airport (SFO), for example. Or, further afield, maybe flying into Brussels and taking a train instead of flying directly into Paris can save you money.

"I want to fly from New York to Paris in February 2027. What nearby departure and arrival airports should I compare? Suggest flexible travel dates and explain which alternative airports have reasonable ground transportation."

ChatGPT suggested a few alternate airports for me in Europe.

Of course, that doesn't really help without seeing the prices. But it will give you some more ideas; you can then check the live prices at Google Flights. Here's where it gets more interesting, though. When I kept pushing the AI tool to find actual deals, it gave me a list of fares to various cities, including Frankfurt and Amsterdam. And when I prodded it again with the prompt, "Anything cheaper if I fly straight to Paris?", it found a couple of better deals.

Those are great deals. Just be sure they are actually bookable. In this case, I did not find the same deal on the FrenchBee website or on Google Flights, but I did find it on Icelandair via Expedia (where Chat had directed me).

So in this case, AI was able to find me an actual deal to Paris, though I likely could have found that same deal by starting my search on Google Flights and avoiding multiple steps. Still, I'm a bit flabbergasted that AI has gotten good enough to find actual flight deals.

With Black Friday almost here, this could be among the most useful ways to use AI.

Airlines love advertising discounts of 20%, 30% or even 50%, but those promotions sometimes apply only to base fares, select dates or specific routes.

AI can help readers understand the fine print and calculate their actual savings.

"I'm considering this Black Friday airfare sale. Analyze the terms and conditions, including blackout dates, excluded routes, baggage charges, booking deadlines and whether the discount applies to the base fare or total ticket price. Tell me what I should verify before booking. Here are the terms: [paste sale details]."

For example, Cathay Pacific has a Black Friday deal on now for "round-trip savings from the U.S. to Hong Kong and destinations across Asia, Australia and New Zealand, with 15% to 25% off Economy, 15% to 30% off Premium Economy and 10% off Business."

I tried to find a round-trip fare from Seattle to Hong Kong, which quoted me $2,687 for premium economy. I then asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal using the prompts above.

ChatGPT told me that, essentially, that wasn't a great deal. When I pressed it to find me a better deal, it couldn't. However, it did find an additional coupon I could use: "promotion code US26BF115 for the additional $115 discount and potential 3,000 bonus Asia Miles."

So when you read the TPG guide to the best Black Friday and Cyber Monday, be sure to ask ChatGPT if it's really a good deal.

Remember that a 40% discount on the base fare doesn't necessarily translate into 40% off the total ticket price.

Want to know if you should use cash or points to pay for your flights? Of course, TPG has a great points and miles calculator, but AI can help, too.

Black Friday airfare sales sometimes make paying cash a better deal than redeeming points and miles.

Readers can use AI to calculate the value of their points and compare cash fares against award tickets.

"I found a Black Friday round-trip flight for $450. The same flight costs 35,000 airline miles plus $50 in taxes. Calculate the cents-per-mile value and explain the trade-offs between paying cash and redeeming miles. Assume both tickets offer comparable benefits."

In this hypothetical example, the redemption yields about 1.14 cents per mile, before accounting for any miles earned on a paid ticket.

Here is a link to TPG's latest points and miles valuations, so you can do your own math, too.

As an illustration, I found a round-trip flight on American Airlines from New York City to Madrid in February for $670. Similar flights cost 60,000 plus $52.09 when booked with miles. I asked ChatGPT if it was a good deal. As you can see, based on TPG valuations, ChatGPT tells me to use cash, not miles.

I've found ChatGPT to be extremely useful in telling me whether to spend cash, miles or points on things like hotels and flights.

Related:10 of our favorite travel hacks from very frequent flyers

Despite my best efforts, AI was not able to find me actual deals for specific flights in most cases. AI still works best as a complement to established flight-search tools, not as a replacement.

Here's an example of a search I tried using Claude's AI. While Black Friday hadn't started yet, it had trouble finding any great deals and didn't show anything in real time.

Of course, I've mentioned Google Flights multiple times, as it's likely your best way to find those flight deals.

Another tool that TPG loves is Points Path. Download it to layer on top of Google Flights to flag good deals on points. Points Path can also send you alerts on good award deals.

For the best results, use award search tools like Seats.aero, Roame.travel or Point.me, alongside AI. You can search for business-class availability and even set alerts to be emailed when the award you are looking for opens.

Related: These new tools will track your flights and get you refunds if the price drops

I track my flights with two other new tools. PAiback has given me back $148 this year alone. I've also been experimenting with Junova. Both companies will monitor cash prices and get you refunds if the price drops, charging you a commission on the money saved.

New users at Junova get a $25 credit when signing up through the TPG referral link (so you get a $25 credit — then when you pay the 20% commission, it comes out of your $25 "bank"). We also like Autopilot.

The point of all this is that, in my experience, AI can't yet find good flight or points deals, though I will keep playing with it. My next move is to try to integrate it with one of my flight deal search companies, but we are not there just yet.

As previously mentioned, there is a lot AI still can't do perfectly. Remember that AI can hallucinate fares, routes, promotions and availability. In most cases, AI chatbots have access to live airline pricing; AI tools may present outdated prices or expired deals. AI-generated fare comparisons may also forget taxes, fees or baggage charges. Finally, even if AI finds you a great trip, the itinerary may disappear before you can book it.

And remember, points and miles deals are still very elusive even with the power of artificial intelligence.

As Potter from Thrifty Traveler told me, "In an age when airlines are getting stingier with award space — and there are more savvy travelers redeeming points than ever before — those great award deals are increasingly dynamic, hinging on new routes or airline capacity changes that can appear and vanish within not just hours but minutes."

In other words, AI won't be able to grab you those incredible deals like companies like Thrifty Traveler can.

Always confirm the final price, itinerary and fare rules before purchasing.

As someone who spends a good chunk of every day searching for flight deals, I've been pleasantly surprised by how far artificial intelligence has come. While I'm not ready to give up my favorite flight search tools, AI has earned a place in my travel-planning arsenal.

Whether you're shopping for Black Friday, Cyber Monday or Travel Tuesday deals, AI can help you think outside the box, identify cheaper destinations and alternative airports, decipher complicated sale terms, and determine whether you're better off paying cash or redeeming points and miles.

Just don't take everything AI tells you at face value. I've encountered plenty of fares that I couldn't actually book, and AI still has a long way to go when it comes to finding award availability.

For now, the sweet spot is combining AI with tried-and-true tools like Google Flights, Points Path and flight deal-alert services. And, as always, flexibility remains your greatest asset when looking for cheap flights.

AI may not be the ultimate travel deal finder just yet, but it could help you become a smarter shopper — and save you some serious cash or miles in the process.
